# Amazon Route 53: say it

<!-- speak:start id=route53-s01 -->
### Prompt 1

**A customer asks.** Why can I not point an A record at the IP address of the load balancer?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Because those IP addresses change when the load balancer scales. An alias record names the load balancer, and Amazon Route 53 follows the changes.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: those IP addresses change, so a fixed A record breaks.

It works like this. As traffic changes, Elastic Load Balancing scales the load balancer.

Then it updates the DNS entry, so the IP addresses can move.

An alias record points to the load balancer itself, not to an address.

Amazon Route 53 detects changes in the load balancer on its own.

So the answers hold the new addresses, and you change nothing.

An alias record also works at callvale.example, where a CNAME record is not allowed.

The thing to watch is customers who want fixed addresses for their firewalls.

An Application Load Balancer has no static addresses. A Network Load Balancer can have them.

In your case, callvale.example and app.callvale.example become alias records to your AWS resources.

Does any customer need fixed IP addresses for an allow list?

**Skeleton.** addresses change when it scales / alias record names the resource / Route 53 follows the changes / fixed addresses need Network Load Balancer

**Must say.**

- Elastic Load Balancing scales the load balancer as traffic changes and updates its DNS entry, so the IP addresses of the load balancer nodes change.
- An alias record points to the AWS resource, and Route 53 detects changes in the resource on its own and answers with the new IP address.
- You can create an alias record at the zone apex, where the DNS protocol does not allow a CNAME record.

**Do not say.**

- "the load balancer's IP addresses never change". Say: Elastic Load Balancing scales the load balancer and updates its DNS entry, so the IP addresses change.
- "use a CNAME record at callvale.example". Say: The DNS protocol does not allow a CNAME record at the zone apex. Use an alias record there.
- "an alias record is the same as a CNAME record". Say: Unlike a CNAME record, an alias record can be created at the zone apex, and it follows the AWS resource.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Can we use a CNAME record for app.callvale.example instead? Yes, a CNAME record is allowed for a subdomain, but not for callvale.example itself. An alias record to the load balancer also works there, and its queries do not incur a charge.
- Which TTL does the alias record use? You cannot set it. If an alias record points to an AWS resource, Route 53 uses the default TTL for the resource.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

<!-- speak:start id=route53-s02 -->
### Prompt 2

**A customer asks.** Latency routing or geolocation routing: which one sends my users to the fastest Region?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Latency routing. It sends each user to the Region with the best latency. Geolocation routing decides by the user's location, not by speed.

**In 60 seconds.**

Both choose a Region for each user.

The difference is the goal: speed, or a fixed place for each location.

It works like this. Latency routing uses latency data between users and AWS data centers.

Amazon Route 53 then sends each user to the Region with the best latency.

Geolocation routing looks at where the DNS query comes from.

It matches that location to the records you create.

Location is sometimes a good guide to speed, and sometimes it is not.

The thing to watch is the default record in geolocation routing.

Without a default record, users from other locations get no answer.

In your case, use latency routing if speed is the goal.

Use geolocation routing when a rule keeps one country's users in one Region.

Do you have a rule like that for any of your customers?

**Skeleton.** both pick a Region / latency routing: best latency / geolocation: user location / no default record, no answer

**Must say.**

- Latency routing sends traffic to the Region that provides the best latency.
- Geolocation routing chooses resources based on where users are located, meaning the location that DNS queries come from.
- To minimize latency AWS recommends latency routing; for compliance or localization that needs stable routing from a geography, geolocation routing.
- If you do not create a default geolocation record, Route 53 returns a no answer response for locations without a record.

**Do not say.**

- "geolocation routing sends each user to the nearest Region". Say: Geolocation routing matches the user's location to the records you create. Latency routing picks the Region with the best latency.
- "latency routing measures how fast your own servers respond". Say: Latency data is based on traffic between users and AWS data centers, not on your own resources.

**Follow-up questions.**

- And what is geoproximity routing? Geoproximity routing uses the location of your resources. You can set a bias, which expands or shrinks the geographic region from which traffic goes to a resource.
- Can latency routing still send users to a Region that is down? Not if you associate a health check with each record. If a health check finds the resource unhealthy, Route 53 routes traffic away from the associated record.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

<!-- speak:start id=route53-s03 -->
### Prompt 3

**A customer asks.** We run in two Regions. If the first Region fails, how does DNS move our users to the second one, and how fast?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Use failover alias records. The primary gets its health from Evaluate Target Health or a health check. Users move when their cached answer expires.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: failover records, with a health signal on the primary Region.

It works like this. You create a primary record and a secondary record.

Health checkers test the primary endpoint every half minute by default.

By default, three failed checks in a row make the primary unhealthy.

Then Amazon Route 53 answers with the secondary record instead.

But resolvers keep the old answer until its TTL runs out.

So keep that TTL at a minute or less.

The thing to watch is your recovery path.

Create the records and health checks in advance. Do not plan to edit records during the outage.

If seconds matter, look at AWS Global Accelerator: its changes propagate in seconds.

In your case, use alias records for the load balancers, with Evaluate Target Health.

How long can your users wait during a failover?

**Skeleton.** primary and secondary records / health check marks primary unhealthy / TTL decides how fast / build it before the outage

**Must say.**

- Failover routing is for active-passive failover: Route 53 routes traffic to a different resource when the first one is unhealthy.
- By default the request interval is 30 seconds and the failure threshold is three health checks.
- Caching resolvers are outside Route 53's control and keep answers for their TTL; with a health check, AWS recommends a TTL of 60 seconds or less.
- Do not rely on the Route 53 control plane in the recovery path; use the status of health checks to fail over.

**Do not say.**

- "users move to the second Region instantly". Say: Caching resolvers keep the old answer according to its TTL, so users move after their cached answer expires.
- "we update the DNS records when the outage happens". Say: Do not rely on the Route 53 control plane in the recovery path. Create failover records and health checks in advance.
- "Route 53 replaces the failed instances". Say: Route 53 routes traffic away from the record of the unhealthy resource. It does not repair the resource.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Our primary is behind a load balancer. Do we need a separate health check? No. Create an alias record that points to the load balancer and set Evaluate Target Health to true.
- What happens if both Regions fail their health checks? Route 53 still answers. If none of the records in a group are healthy, Route 53 considers all of them healthy and selects one based on the routing policy.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

<!-- speak:start id=route53-s04 -->
### Prompt 4

**A customer asks.** Our domain is registered with another company. Do we have to move it to AWS to use Route 53?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** No. You keep the registration where it is. You create a hosted zone, and your registrar points the domain to the zone's name servers.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is no: you can keep the domain at your registrar.

It works like this. You create a public hosted zone in Amazon Route 53.

You copy your DNS records into that hosted zone.

Amazon Route 53 gives the hosted zone a unique set of four name servers.

At your registrar, you replace the old name servers with those four.

After that, resolvers ask Amazon Route 53 for your records.

The thing to watch is caching during the switch.

Resolvers remember the old name servers for some time.

So first lower the TTL of the NS record at both DNS providers.

If something is missing, you can then go back with less downtime.

In your case, check that every record is in the hosted zone before the switch.

Who on your team can sign in to the registrar today?

**Skeleton.** keep the registrar / hosted zone, copy records / registrar gets four name servers / lower NS TTL first

**Must say.**

- Transferring the domain registration to Route 53 is not required to use other Route 53 features.
- If another registrar keeps the domain, you ask the registrar to update the name servers to the ones of your hosted zone.
- By default, Route 53 assigns a unique set of four name servers to each hosted zone that you create.
- Lowering the TTL for the NS record, both at the current DNS provider and in Route 53, reduces downtime if you find a problem during the migration.

**Do not say.**

- "you must transfer the domain to AWS first". Say: Transferring the domain registration to Route 53 is not required to use other Route 53 features.
- "the switch reaches every user within a minute". Say: Caching resolvers keep records according to their TTL, so lower the TTL of the NS record before the switch.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Can we move the registration to Route 53 later? Yes. If you registered the domain with another registrar, you can transfer the domain registration to Route 53. It is a separate step from moving DNS.
- After the switch, does a record change in Route 53 reach users right away? Changes generally propagate to all Route 53 servers within 60 seconds. Resolvers still keep the old answer until its TTL ends.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->
